newsitem.title: USA: Fed criticized for allowing outsiders at meetings.
newsitem.headline: Fed criticized for allowing outsiders at meetings.

text.p: Two members of the U.S. House Banking Committee expressed concern to Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan on Monday about outsiders attending monetary policy meetings.

"We are deeply troubled to learn from Chairman Greenspan that while the Fed publicly feigns horror about published leaks from its private monetary policy meetings, it has and continues to invite an elite group to its monetary policy discussions," ranking House Banking Committee member Henry Gonzalez, D-NY, said in a letter to Greenspan.
Reuters obtained a copy of the letter.
"This group -- "Club Fed" -- ranges from visiting scholars to representatives of foreign government," the letter, co-authored by House Banking Committee member Maurice Hinchey, D- NY, also said.
"We find it troubling that where the door is closed for Congressional oversight, many people who are not even employees of the Federal Reserve are welcome," the letter further said.

The lawmakers said Greenspan, in an April 25, 1997, letter to Gonzalez in response to a query from Gonzalez, admitted "that secret Federal Reserve meetings at the 12 Federal Reserve Banks were attended by a variety of individuals including foreign bankers and visiting scholars."

-- Twenty-eight representatives of foreign countries, from China to Hungary, "attended the Fed's Board of Directors' meetings that included discussion and votes on discount rates" at the Kansas City Fed.
-- The Chicago Fed "allowed a non-employee of the bank to attend their top-secret meetings just before the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) met in Washington,"
-- "Economists who are not employees of the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta attended pre-FOMC meetings,"
-- "Surely, the Fed can change its policy of waiting five years to release verbatim minutes of the FOMC,"
-- The full transcript of the FOMC meetings should be made public "with no more than a one-year delay."
